description: We are a team of young students attending a technical institute for computer science, eager to take on new challenges.
summary:
SpaceAccademy is a browser-based space mission design game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge "Space Mission Design Game". Players pick a mission (orbital test, satellite launch, Moon or Mars landing), choose launcher, destination and spacecraft components, and watch mass, power, budget, data, communications, time and environmental impact change in real time. A compatibility check, a simulated mission with unexpected events and a final report close the loop.

It addresses the challenge by making trade-offs visible: every choice has a consequence, there is no single perfect design, and a "Why?" panel explains what happened, why, which official data it relies on and what alternatives exist. Three levels (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced) change the language and depth, not the science, so students and engineers can play the same mission.

It matters because it teaches real mission engineering with real data, rewards sustainable choices (reused parts, responsible end of life, lower launch emissions) and bold, non-standard designs, and every value is traceable to a source.
details:
What it does and how it works. SpaceAccademy guides the player through a complete mission: nickname and level, NASA base, mission choice (orbital test, satellite launch, Moon or Mars landing, suborbital flight, rover or probe), fixed and extra objectives, spacecraft design (launcher, destination, power, communications, instruments), a pre-launch compatibility check, a phase-by-phase simulation with unexpected events, and a final report saved to a local history. A dashboard shows value, limit and change after the last choice for mass, power, budget, data, communications, time and environmental impact. Clicking any value opens the "Why?" panel: what happened, why, which official source supports it, and what the alternatives are. Every component has an (i) symbol that explains its function, its effect on the parameters and, if it is reused or made of sustainable material, where it comes from.

Benefits. Players learn that space engineering is a chain of trade-offs, without being told which answer is right: a Mission Advisor only points out what does not add up and asks questions. Three levels (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced) tell the same mission in different language and detail, so a student and an engineer use the same game. The Advanced level shows the mathematics used, such as the rocket equation, and the final report lists assumptions, margins and sources, so it can be a starting point for a preliminary analysis.

Intended impact. To make mission design understandable for a wide audience and to put environmental impact next to cost and mass as a real design constraint. Choosing a reused part, a launcher with a recovered first stage or a responsible end of life always improves the score, and the game explains why and what it costs.

Tools and technologies. Vite, React and TypeScript for the web app. The calculation engine is a separate TypeScript module with pure functions, independent from the interface. All scientific values live in JSON data files, each with a source identifier. A small Node.js server saves reports as local files; the game works offline. Vitest for automated tests of the compatibility check and the score. SVG for the vehicle schematic. Team documentation in Google Docs and Google Sheets. AI assistance: Claude and Claude Code were used to draft documentation and generate code from our functional and technical analysis.

Creativity. A Courage parameter rewards valid missions that differ from real-mission norms. A Mission Advisor asks questions instead of giving solutions. A leaf symbol and a "Why is it better?" panel explain every ecological choice. A team mode for up to four roles in conflict is shown as a preview of the future.

Factors we considered. Scientific fidelity: no invented values; where an official value is missing, the game uses an estimate computed from similar cases, labelled ESTIMATE, with its method and sources. Accessibility across levels. Environmental impact of launch, end of life and surface. Stability of the live demo, offline. Very limited development time, so we fixed priorities and built the Intermediate level and the orbital test and landing missions first.
